title.narrative: BCSDN Regional Civil Society Development Hub 2023-27
BCSDN Regional Civil Society Development Hub 2023-27

description.narrative: BCSDN är ett nätverk med 13 civilsamhällesorganisationer (CSOs) i den vidare Balkan-regionen. BCSDN verkar för att stärka civilsamhället och att påverka europeiska och nationella policys och program för en bättre tillvaro för civilsamhället som i förlängningen syftar till att säkerställa fungerande och hållbara demokratier i regionen. Sida ger stöd till BCSDN's Hub, som är en del av det bredare BCSDN-nätverket som syftar till att öka samarbete och motståndskraft hos civilsamhällesorganisationer på västra Balkan (Albanien, Bosnien-Hercegovina, Kosovo, Montenegro, Nordmakedonien, Serbien). Programmet arbetar mot tre huvudsakliga mål: effektivt evidensbaserat påverkansarbete, ökad förståelse för vikten av en möjliggörande miljö för civila samhället att verka samt starkare regionalt samarbete för civilsamhället. Programmet stödjer bland annat arbetet med att analysera och "mäta" utrymmet för det civila samhället att verka i regionen. Slutsatserna från dessa studier används i nätverkets påverkansarbete på nationell, regional och EU-nivå. Även om BCSDN Hub framför allt handlar om västra Balkan-regionen med ovan nämna länder, ingår Turkiet i viss mån genom regionalt utbyte och gemensamt påverkansarbete.

The Balkan Civil Society Development Network is a network of 13 civil society organizations from the wider Balkan region. Its mission is to empower civil society and influence European and national policies towards a more enabling environment for civil society development to ensure sustainable and functioning democracies in the Balkans. Sida supports the BCSDN Hub, which is a program within the wider BCSDN’s work. The Hub aims to enhance the cooperation and resilience of civil society organisations in the Western Balkans. More specifically, the Hub works within the current program towards three immediate outcomes: effective evidence-based advocacy for civic space, increased understanding of the enabling environment, and stronger regional cooperation for civic space. Among other things, the Hub supports the monitoring of the enabling environment for civil society in the Western Balkan countries and use the findings for advocacy at country, regional, and EU-levels. The BCSDN Hub focuses on the Western Balkan 6 countries to which most of the funds go, but Türkiye is participating in regional exchange and joint advocacy work.

Ultimate outcome/impact: Enhanced cooperation and resilience of CSOs in the Western Balkan countries that contribute to open civic space.
Intermediate outcomes Positive changes in standards and legislation affecting the Enabling Environment for Civil Society Increased common understanding and cooperation for promoting civic space.
Immediate outcomes: Evidence-based advocacy for promoting the enabling environment and civic space Improved awareness of key stakeholders about enabling environment standards and civic space state of play in the Western Balkans Strengthened CSO and multi-stakeholder collaboration for protecting the civic space.

Examples of direct results/outputs:
Reports published as results of BCSDNs analyses and research, such as the Monitoring Matrix reports on the enabling environment in the Western Balkans (country and regional) and other in-depth research reports such as on SLAPPs in the region and on civic space and gender equality. The research and reports have been used as a basis for advocacy towards national governments and EU stakeholders by BCSDN and its members as well as other civil society organisations.
Various advocacy events and efforts have been conducted by BCSDN and its members. BCSDN has facilitated strategic advocacy action and responses to repressive measures by members and other civil society actors through its research, reports, rapid alerts, and communication (such as the updated Monitoring Matrix website). By positioning civic space as a fundamental benchmark of EU accession, BCSDN ensured that its Monitoring Matrix, policy briefs, and regional evidence informed high-level policy dialogues, including the Berlin Process, EESC Enlargement Forums, and the OGP agenda.
BCSDN has facilitated networking and collaboration between civil society actors for protecting civic space through regional coalitions, working groups, and joint actions that addressed threats to civic space in the Western Balkans. The redesigned Civic Space Fund enabled targeted support for coalition-driven initiatives, including small action grants that resulted in legal aid, awareness campaigns, national workshops, and policy papers across Albania, Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Montenegro. The organization of the first Civic Space Hackathon in 2025 showcased innovative responses to disinformation, smear campaigns, and funding restrictions, reinforcing the value of multi-stakeholder engagement in developing creative solutions.
Examples of changed behaviour, action, policies etc by key actors:
EU institutions used findings of the Monitoring Matrix as a benchmarking and verification tool in policy discussions and as reference in policy documents. The Monitoring Matrix was referenced in key EU documents such as the EU Commission country reports and IPA Civil Society Facility programming for Albania and North Macedonia. The European Economic and Social Committee (EESC) recognized BCSDNs monitoring as instrumental in informing the EUs approach to supporting an enabling environment for civil society in the Western Balkans and used BCSDNs findings in its official opinion. The EESC also continued its initiative of involving civil society and social partners from the enlargement countries in opinions, and included the direct involvement of Kosovo civil society representatives. BCSDNs advocacy contributed to this decision.
Members of the European Parliament (MEPs) and the Cabinet of the Enlargement Commissioner have changed their rhetoric and messaging around civic space after BCSDN's advocacy. At the outset of BCSDNs urgent advocacy visit to Brussels in October 2024 on the situation in Serbia, many EU stakeholders were dismissive of the severity of the crackdown on civic space, with only a few key MEPs (mainly from the Greens) acknowledging the urgency. Following BCSDNs interventions including policy briefs, Enlargement Package analysis, and coordinated advocacy at EU fora momentum visibly shifted. The same MEPs began hosting and participating in follow-up events, helping bring Serbia's civic space crisis into the spotlight. By the time of BCSDNs high-level advocacy mission later that autumn, EU discourse had changed: civic space and democratic regression were consistently acknowledged in discussions with diverse decision-makers and shapers. This shift culminated when, just days after BCSDNs meetings with the Cabinet of Commissioner Kos, the Commissioner released a video statement on World NGO Day underscoring the importance of NGOs, zero tolerance for actions undermining civil society, and the need for stronger EU support to civic space in the Western Balkans.
Civil society actors across the Western Balkans networked, enhanced each others messages, and mobilized joint advocacy actions, as a result of BCSDNs facilitation of the collaboration between civil society actors and by providing a platform for civic space issues in the region.
